genres.name: Kraftwerk: Autobahn
genres.text: In November 1974 Kraftwerk, from Düsseldorf, released the album Autobahn. The title track lasts over twenty minutes and sounds like a drive along the motorway, made with synthesizers, electronic drums and a voice through a vocoder. A shortened version became a hit in America. Synthpop, electro, hip-hop and techno owe a great deal to this German band.
genres.listen: The song begins with the sound of a car starting and driving off. Hear how Fahr'n, fahr'n, fahr'n auf der Autobahn sounds like a cheerful jingle, yet almost everything is electronic.

genres.name: The Warehouse in Chicago
genres.text: In March 1977 the club The Warehouse opened in a factory building in Chicago. DJ Frankie Knuckles came from New York and played disco, soul and European electronic records there all night. With a tape recorder he cut songs longer and harder. The crowd was mostly black and gay. Record shops later wrote 'as heard at the Warehouse' on their bins. That is how house got its name.
genres.listen: Your Love was written by the singer Jamie Principle, and Knuckles only released his own version in 1987. Hear the dreamy synthesizer melody that runs through the whole song, over a dry drum machine rhythm.

genres.name: Donna Summer: I Feel Love
genres.text: In the summer of 1977 I Feel Love came out, sung by Donna Summer and made by Giorgio Moroder in Munich. Apart from the voice and the bass drum, everything is played on a Moog synthesizer, with a bassline that ticks on like a machine. Brian Eno told David Bowie this was the sound of the future. He was right: the dance music of the 1980s starts here.
genres.listen: Listen to the bass: fast, endlessly repeated notes from a sequencer that never gets tired. Donna Summer's voice floats high and soft above it.

genres.name: The Blitz Club
genres.text: At the start of 1979 Steve Strange and Rusty Egan began a Tuesday night at the Blitz, a wine bar in London. Strange stood at the door and only let in people who had dressed spectacularly, as a pirate, a dandy or a Pierrot. Egan played Bowie, Kraftwerk and Roxy Music. Boy George worked in the cloakroom, and Spandau Ballet played there. Newspapers called the visitors New Romantics.
genres.listen: Visage was the band of Steve Strange and Rusty Egan themselves. Hear the cool synthesizers and the whispered French of a woman's voice.

genres.name: Margaret Thatcher becomes prime minister
genres.text: On 4 May 1979 Margaret Thatcher became the first female prime minister of Great Britain. She closed coal mines and factories, and unemployment rose above three million. Many musicians saw her as an opponent and sang against her policies. Together with Ronald Reagan, president of America from 1981, she gave the decade its colour: free market, making money and a hard line towards the Soviet Union.
genres.listen: The Beat from Birmingham turned their protest into a danceable ska song. The title says it all: Stand Down Margaret, step down.

genres.name: Tubeway Army and Gary Numan
genres.text: In the summer of 1979 Tubeway Army reached number one in England with Are 'Friends' Electric? Singer Gary Numan had found a Minimoog in the studio that someone had left behind, and discovered how heavy it sounded. On television he stood stiffly, in white make-up, like a robot. He then carried on alone with Cars. Everyone could now see that with a synthesizer you could become a pop star.
genres.listen: Hear how Are 'Friends' Electric? builds up slowly, with a synthesizer line that keeps returning and almost no chorus. In Cars the synthesizer is right at the front.

genres.name: The Sony Walkman
genres.text: On 1 July 1979 Sony released the Walkman in Japan: a cassette player not much bigger than a paperback, with light headphones. For the first time you took your own music everywhere, out on the street, onto the bus. The first model even had two headphone sockets, so you could listen together. Sony sold tens of millions of them, and the mixtape became something to carry with you.

genres.name: The Fairlight CMI
genres.text: In 1979 the Fairlight CMI came out of Australia, a computer with a keyboard and a light pen with which you could draw on the screen. Most importantly, it could record sounds and play them back at any pitch. A sampler, in other words. It cost as much as a house, but Peter Gabriel, Kate Bush and Trevor Horn had to have one. The orchestral sound ORCH5 became one of the best-known sounds of the 1980s.
genres.listen: Kate Bush was one of the first to use the Fairlight, on her 1980 album Never for Ever. At the end of Babooshka, hear the breaking glass: a recorded sound played back by the Fairlight.

genres.name: Video Killed the Radio Star
genres.text: In September 1979 Video Killed the Radio Star was released by The Buggles, the duo of Trevor Horn and Geoff Downes. The song is about a singer whose career is wiped out by television. Horn got the idea from a science fiction story by J.G. Ballard. It became a number one in England and in many other countries. Two years later it was the very first video that MTV broadcast.
genres.listen: Hear the high girls' voices in the background and the thin radio sound at the beginning. Horn made it into a farewell letter to the radio.

genres.name: Rapper's Delight
genres.text: In September 1979 Sylvia Robinson of the small label Sugar Hill Records released Rapper's Delight by The Sugarhill Gang, three rappers she had quickly put together in Englewood, New Jersey. They rapped for almost fifteen minutes over the bassline of Good Times by Chic. Those who had been rapping in the Bronx for years were amazed. But the record became a worldwide hit and let a large audience hear for the first time what hip-hop was.
genres.listen: The music was replayed by a studio band, not sampled. Listen to how the three rappers take turns, each with their own voice and their own jokes.

genres.name: Geen woning, geen kroning
genres.text: On 30 April 1980 Beatrix was inaugurated as queen in the Nieuwe Kerk in Amsterdam. Squatters protested against the housing shortage with the slogan Geen woning, geen kroning. In the streets around the Dam there were hours of fighting with the riot police, while inside the ceremony went on. Around the squats a music world of its own grew, with punk bands, rehearsal rooms and squat pubs. In the 1980s the Netherlands was not only cheerful Nederpop.

genres.name: Joy Division becomes New Order
genres.text: On 18 May 1980, just before Joy Division's first American tour, the singer Ian Curtis took his own life in Macclesfield. He was 23. A month later Love Will Tear Us Apart came out and became a hit. The other three band members carried on under a new name: New Order. They gradually let go of the dark guitars and chose synthesizers and dance rhythms.
genres.listen: Hear the tight drums of Stephen Morris and the low, flat voice of Curtis. The lyrics are about a marriage falling apart, but the music simply carries on.

genres.name: The Roland TR-808
genres.text: In 1980 Roland of Japan released the TR-808, a drum machine with which you could programme your own rhythms. The drums did not sound real at all: the bass drum boomed on for a long time, the handclap sounded like plastic and the cowbell tinkled. Musicians did not think much of it, and after a few years production stopped. But second-hand the machine was cheap. That is how the 808 ended up in electro, hip-hop and later house.
genres.listen: Sexual Healing was one of the first big hits with the 808. Hear the ticking rhythms and the soft, round sound of the drum machine beneath Marvin Gaye's voice.

genres.name: AC/DC: Back in Black
genres.text: In February 1980 Bon Scott, the singer of AC/DC, died. The band took on a new singer, Brian Johnson, and flew to the Bahamas to record. Back in Black came out on 25 July 1980, with an all-black sleeve in mourning for Scott. It became one of the best-selling albums ever: hard rock without frills, with loud guitars, a tight rhythm and not a synthesizer in sight.
genres.listen: Hear Angus Young's guitar riff and how much space there is between the notes. The drums play almost boringly straight ahead, and that is exactly what makes it so heavy.

genres.name: John Lennon murdered
genres.text: On the evening of 8 December 1980 John Lennon was shot dead in front of his apartment building, The Dakota, in New York, by a man to whom he had given an autograph that same afternoon. Three weeks earlier Double Fantasy had been released, his first album in five years. All over the world people gathered to sing his songs. For many it felt like the end of the sixties.
genres.listen: Starting Over was the first single from Double Fantasy, a cheerful song in the style of the fifties. After his death it suddenly sounded very different.

genres.name: The first reports of AIDS
genres.text: On 5 June 1981 the American health institute CDC reported five cases of a rare pneumonia in young gay men in Los Angeles. It was the first report of the disease that would later be called AIDS. In the years that followed many musicians, dancers, designers and DJs died of AIDS. In Sign o' the Times from 1987 Prince sang about a man who dies of a big disease with a small name.
genres.listen: The song is almost bare: a drum machine, a bass loop and Prince's voice. He sings about AIDS, drugs, gangs and an exploded space shuttle, the news of the day.

genres.name: Home Taping Is Killing Music
genres.text: In 1981 the British record industry began a campaign against recording music on cassette: Home Taping Is Killing Music, with a cassette as a skull. With a double cassette recorder anyone could copy records and make mixtapes for friends. As early as 1980 the band Bow Wow Wow had released a single that came out only on cassette, with a blank side for recording something yourself.
genres.listen: C30 C60 C90 Go! says you should record music from the radio instead of buying it. Hear the wild drums, borrowed from the drummers of Burundi.

genres.name: The Roland TB-303
genres.text: In 1981 Roland released the TB-303 Bass Line, a small silver box that was meant to imitate a bass guitar. Guitarists could programme a bassline with it at home to practise to. But it did not sound like a bass guitar at all, and it was hard to operate. After a few years Roland stopped making it. Later the boxes lay in the second-hand shops of Chicago for next to nothing.

genres.name: MTV begins
genres.text: On 1 August 1981, just after midnight, MTV began in America, a television channel that broadcast music videos all day. The first words were: Ladies and gentlemen, rock and roll. The first video was Video Killed the Radio Star. At first very few people could receive the channel. Within a few years MTV became the place where hits were made, and every artist had to look good.

genres.name: Soft Cell: Tainted Love
genres.text: In September 1981 Soft Cell from Leeds were at number one in England with Tainted Love, a forgotten soul song by Gloria Jones from 1964 that was popular in the Northern Soul clubs. Marc Almond sang and Dave Ball played everything on synthesizers and a drum machine. The duo showed that an electronic band could also have soul, feeling and glamour. In America the record stayed in the chart for a record length of time.
genres.listen: Hear the tink-tink of the synthesizer at the beginning. Compare it with the version by Gloria Jones, which sounds much faster and more cheerful.

genres.name: The Human League: Don't You Want Me
genres.text: In November 1981 Don't You Want Me came out by The Human League from Sheffield. Singer Phil Oakey had discovered two girls, Joanne Catherall and Susan Ann Sulley, in a disco and simply asked them to join the band. Producer Martin Rushent built the song up with synthesizers and a drum machine. It became the Christmas number one in England. Synthpop was no longer something for nerds: it was the new pop.
genres.listen: The song is an argument between two people: first Oakey sings, then Susan Ann Sulley answers with her side of the story.

genres.name: Demonstration against cruise missiles
genres.text: On 21 November 1981 some 400,000 people marched in Amsterdam in a demonstration against the deployment of American cruise missiles in the Netherlands. In 1983 even more came in The Hague. All over Europe people were afraid of a nuclear war between America and the Soviet Union. That fear also sounded through the music, from Nena in Germany and Righeira in Italy to Doe Maar in the Netherlands.

genres.name: The Commodore 64
genres.text: In January 1982 Commodore showed the Commodore 64 at a trade fair in Las Vegas. It became the best-selling home computer ever. Inside the computer was a clever sound chip, the SID, with three voices. Composers such as Rob Hubbard and Martin Galway made game music with it that many children knew better than the charts. All over Europe teenagers swapped games and music on cassettes.

genres.name: Iron Maiden: The Number of the Beast
genres.text: On 29 March 1982 The Number of the Beast by Iron Maiden was released in England, the first album with singer Bruce Dickinson. It reached number one in the British album chart. Iron Maiden was the leader of the New Wave of British Heavy Metal: young British bands who played metal faster and rougher. In America Christian groups accused the band of devil worship, and in some places their records were burned.
genres.listen: Run to the Hills begins with galloping drums. The song tells of the expulsion of the Native Americans, first from their side and then from the soldiers' side.

genres.name: Afrika Bambaataa: Planet Rock
genres.text: In April 1982 the small label Tommy Boy released Planet Rock by Afrika Bambaataa & the Soulsonic Force. Bambaataa was a DJ from the Bronx who also played Kraftwerk. Producer Arthur Baker and keyboard player John Robie took the melody of Trans-Europe Express and the rhythm of Numbers, and put an 808 underneath. That is how electro began: hip-hop with the sound of the future. In England, Detroit and Miami the record was played to death.
genres.listen: Hear the 808 drums and the melody of Kraftwerk. Compare Planet Rock with Trans-Europe Express: the same melody, but a completely different world.

genres.name: Duran Duran on a yacht
genres.text: In 1982 Duran Duran flew to Sri Lanka and Antigua to shoot videos. In the video for Rio, Simon Le Bon sings on the bow of a sailing yacht, in pastel-coloured suits by the designer Antony Price. It cost a lot of money, but it earned even more. Such a video was an advertisement for the band, and MTV played it again and again. Duran Duran became big in America thanks to television.
genres.listen: Hear John Taylor's bass, which pushes the whole song forward, and the saxophone solo in the middle.

genres.name: The Message
genres.text: On 1 July 1982 The Message came out by Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five. Until then rap had mostly been about parties and boasting. Melle Mel now rapped about life in the Bronx: broken glass, rats, debts and violence. The chorus says he is close to the edge. It was the first big rap record that told how things really were. After The Message, hip-hop could also be news.
genres.listen: The rhythm is slow and heavy, made with synthesizers and a drum machine. Listen to the end: the rappers are arrested by the police.

genres.name: The compact disc
genres.text: On 17 August 1982 the first compact discs for the shops were made in a factory in Langenhagen near Hanover. One of the first was The Visitors by ABBA. Philips of Eindhoven and Sony had developed the little disc together. A CD had no hiss, no scratches and fitted in your hand. On 1 October 1982 the first CD players were in the shops in Japan. A few years later the CD displaced the LP.
genres.listen: On The Visitors, their last album before a break of almost forty years, ABBA sounds cool and electronic. The title song is about someone in the Soviet Union who is afraid of a visit from the secret police.

genres.name: Doe Maar: De Bom
genres.text: Doe Maar was the biggest band in the Netherlands in 1982 and 1983. At gigs girls screamed as they once had for the Beatles. In November 1982 De Bom came out, in which Henny Vrienten sang about the fear of nuclear war, to a bouncing ska rhythm. It became a number one and the whole country cheerfully sang along about the end of the world. In 1984 the band stopped, because the craze around the group had grown too big.
genres.listen: Hear the rhythms from reggae and ska, which Doe Maar took from Jamaica and from 2 Tone, while the lyrics are about the last day.

genres.name: Michael Jackson: Thriller
genres.text: On 30 November 1982 Thriller by Michael Jackson was released, produced by Quincy Jones. Of the nine songs, seven became a Top 10 hit in America. The album spent 37 weeks at number one and became the best-selling album of all time, with an estimated seventy million copies. Jackson became the biggest star in the world, and the music industry saw how much money could be made with one record.
genres.listen: Beat It mixes funk and rock: the guitar solo is by Eddie Van Halen, who wanted nothing for it. That way Jackson reached rock fans too.

genres.name: MIDI
genres.text: At the NAMM show in Anaheim in January 1983 a synthesizer from Sequential Circuits and one from Roland were connected with a single cable. What you played on one sounded on the other. That was MIDI, a language that the brands had agreed on together. After that, one computer could control a whole band of synthesizers and drum machines. More than forty years later MIDI is still in use.

genres.name: Nena: 99 Luftballons
genres.text: In January 1983 99 Luftballons came out by the German band Nena. The song tells how 99 balloons in the sky are mistaken for UFOs, after which armies send fighter planes and a war begins. It is a cheerful pop song about the end of the world. It became a hit all over Europe and even, in German, in America. Nena belongs to the Neue Deutsche Welle: new pop music in German.
genres.listen: It begins quietly, with only a synthesizer and Nena's voice, and then speeds up. Listen for the ending: everything falls silent again.

genres.name: New Order: Blue Monday
genres.text: On 7 March 1983 New Order released Blue Monday, only as a 12-inch single. The song lasts over seven minutes and begins with a drum machine that rattles like a machine gun. The sleeve looked like a floppy disk with holes and was so expensive that the label Factory lost money on the first copies. Even so it became the best-selling 12-inch ever. Rock and club music came together here.
genres.listen: Listen to the beginning: just the drum machine. Then come the synthesizers and Peter Hook's bass, which he plays high, almost like a guitar.

genres.name: Billie Jean on MTV
genres.text: In the beginning MTV played almost only white rock music. Black artists hardly appeared on it. According to the head of the record company CBS, the channel at first did not want to show Billie Jean either, until he threatened to pull all his artists from MTV. In March 1983 the video went into rotation after all, with the pavement lighting up at every step Jackson took. After that Prince and others also appeared on MTV.
genres.listen: Hear how the drums and the bass together make a tight, creeping rhythm from the very first beat, before Jackson starts to sing.

genres.name: Golden Earring in America
genres.text: At the start of 1983 Golden Earring from The Hague reached the American Top 10 with Twilight Zone, about a secret agent who is hunted down. The video, with spies, pistols and a woman in black leather, was shown often on MTV. Radar Love had already been a hit in America in 1974, but Twilight Zone went even higher. Without the videos on MTV that probably would not have worked.
genres.listen: Hear the long intro with the menacing guitar. Guitarist George Kooymans got the idea for the lyrics from a spy novel.

genres.name: The moonwalk
genres.text: On 25 March 1983 Michael Jackson performed during the recording of the television show Motown 25. After a medley with his brothers he sang only Billie Jean. Halfway through he glided backwards across the stage while it looked as if he was walking forwards: the moonwalk. When the show was broadcast on 16 May, tens of millions of Americans watched. The next day children practised it in school playgrounds.

genres.name: Flashdance
genres.text: On 15 April 1983 the film Flashdance came to the cinema, about a female welder from Pittsburgh who wants to become a ballet dancer. The film was full of dance scenes set to pop music, which looked like music videos. Giorgio Moroder wrote the music of the title song Flashdance... What a Feeling, and the singer Irene Cara wrote the lyrics together with Keith Forsey. It won an Oscar. After that every Hollywood film wanted a soundtrack full of hits, from Footloose to Top Gun.
genres.listen: The song begins softly with synthesizers and grows fuller and louder. Hear Moroder's drum machine and synthesizers, familiar from I Feel Love.

genres.name: Italo disco
genres.text: In the summer of 1983 Vamos a la playa by the Italian duo Righeira sounded on every beach in Europe. It sounds like a holiday song, but the Spanish lyrics are about a beach after an atom bomb, where the radiation colours everything. It belongs to italo disco: Italian dance music with synthesizers, often in English with an accent, made in small studios in northern Italy. Ryan Paris and Gazebo also scored with it.
genres.listen: Compare the two: Righeira sings in Spanish, Ryan Paris in English. Hear the typical sound of italo: a bouncing synthesizer bass and a sunny melody.

genres.name: The Yamaha DX7
genres.text: In 1983 Yamaha released the DX7, one of the first digital synthesizers and one of the first with MIDI. It was much cheaper than earlier synthesizers and sounded bright, with glittering bells, an electric piano and a solid bass. More than a hundred thousand were sold. In very many hits of the 1980s there is a DX7 somewhere, especially the electric piano in ballads.
genres.listen: In Take My Breath Away by Berlin from 1986 the DX7 plays the deep, pulsing bassline that carries the whole song. It is the factory sound Bass 2, straight out of the box.

genres.name: Van Halen: Jump
genres.text: At the end of 1983 Van Halen released Jump. Fans knew the band for Eddie Van Halen's lightning-fast guitar solos, but this song begins with a synthesizer and a cheerful little riff. Singer David Lee Roth saw little in it, but it became their only number one in America. Even hard rock bands now allowed keyboards. In 1985 Roth left the band.
genres.listen: Hear the synthesizer chords at the beginning, played on an Oberheim. Only in the middle does the guitar solo come, short and lightning fast.

genres.name: Relax banned
genres.text: On 11 January 1984 DJ Mike Read said on BBC Radio 1 that he no longer wanted to play Relax by Frankie Goes to Hollywood, because he found the lyrics too sexual. The BBC then banned the song altogether. The ban worked as advertising: the record spent five weeks at number one. Producer Trevor Horn had worked on the sound for months, with sequencers and a Fairlight.
genres.listen: Horn had the music largely replayed by other musicians. Listen to the booming bass and the banging effects.

genres.name: The first house record
genres.text: In January 1984 DJ Jesse Saunders of Chicago released On and On on his own label. He made it together with Vince Lawrence, with a drum machine and a few synthesizers, without a band or a big studio. It is often regarded as the first house record on vinyl. Many young men with cheap equipment and a label of their own followed. Trax and DJ International became the best known. House was do-it-yourself music, like punk.

genres.name: Pepsi and Michael Jackson
genres.text: At the end of 1983 Michael Jackson and his brothers signed an advertising contract with Pepsi for five million dollars, the biggest ever for artists. On 27 January 1984, while a commercial was being filmed, his hair caught fire from fireworks. Jackson suffered serious burns. Even so the collaboration went on. In the 1980s pop and advertising grew towards each other: soft drink and beer brands paid for tours.

genres.name: Free Nelson Mandela
genres.text: In March 1984 The Special AKA, the new name of The Specials from Coventry, released Free Nelson Mandela. Mandela had by then been in prison in South Africa for more than twenty years, because he had fought against apartheid. Jerry Dammers had only heard of him shortly before. The cheerful song became an anthem of the anti-apartheid movement. Millions of young people now knew Mandela's name.
genres.listen: The song sounds like a party, with influences from South African music and cheerful brass. Elvis Costello produced the record.

genres.name: Bronski Beat: Smalltown Boy
genres.text: On 25 May 1984 Bronski Beat released Smalltown Boy. Singer Jimmy Somerville sings in a high voice about a boy who leaves home, because he is gay and is not understood there. In the video he flirts with a swimmer, who then beats him up with his friends. Bronski Beat was one of the first bands to sing openly about being gay. In the Netherlands the song reached number one.
genres.listen: Hear Somerville's high falsetto and the synthesizer melody that keeps returning. Run away, turn away is advice and complaint at the same time.

genres.name: Born in the U.S.A.
genres.text: On 4 June 1984 Born in the U.S.A. by Bruce Springsteen was released. The title song sounds like a festive anthem, but is about a Vietnam veteran who gets no work and no help at home. When President Reagan praised Springsteen in his election campaign, Springsteen answered mockingly at a concert and then played a sombre song about unemployment. Seven songs from the album became a Top 10 hit.
genres.listen: Listen to the words in the verses and compare them with the chorus: what sounds like pride is really anger.

genres.name: Breakdance in Europe
genres.text: In the summer of 1984 Beat Street came to the cinema, a film about young people from the Bronx who rap, spray graffiti and breakdance. All over Europe teenagers afterwards began spinning on pieces of cardboard or linoleum in the street, with a ghetto blaster beside them. In the Netherlands too, breakdance contests were held. That is how hip-hop came to Europe first as dance and graffiti, and only later as rap.
genres.listen: Beat Street Breakdown by Melle Mel is the title song of the film. Hear the electronic drums and the scratches, made for dancing to.

tracks.artist: Grandmaster Melle Mel, The Furious Five & Grandmaster Flash
tracks.title: Beat Street Breakdown

genres.name: Two Tribes
genres.text: In June 1984 came Two Tribes by Frankie Goes to Hollywood, about a nuclear war between two powers. In the video lookalikes of President Reagan and Soviet leader Chernenko fight in a wrestling ring. You hear the voice of the actor Patrick Allen, who, as in real British government films, explains what to do after an atomic attack. The song spent nine weeks at number one, with Relax right below it.
genres.listen: Hear the bass that rolls forward like a tank. The actor Patrick Allen speaks the warnings, just as in the real information films Protect and Survive that he had earlier narrated for the British government.

genres.name: Prince: Purple Rain
genres.text: On 27 July 1984 Purple Rain had its premiere, a film with Prince in the leading role as a young musician in Minneapolis. The music had been released a month earlier as an album and spent 24 weeks at number one in America. The title song was recorded live at First Avenue, the club from the film. Prince could do funk, rock and soul at once, and on many records played almost everything himself.
genres.listen: When Doves Cry has no bass guitar. Prince took the bass out at the last moment, and that is exactly why the song sounds bare and strange.

genres.name: Madonna at the MTV Awards

place.name: New York, Radio City Music Hall

genres.text: On 14 September 1984 the first MTV Video Music Awards were held in New York. Madonna sang Like a Virgin on top of an enormous wedding cake, in a wedding dress. She lost a shoe, rolled across the floor and simply carried on. The audience was shocked and her manager thought her career was over. The opposite happened: Madonna showed that with image and uproar you could become a star.
genres.listen: Producer Nile Rodgers, of Chic, gave the song a tight funk bass, which is reminiscent of Billie Jean.

genres.name: Band Aid
genres.text: In October 1984 Bob Geldof saw a report on the BBC about the famine in Ethiopia. Together with Midge Ure of Ultravox he wrote Do They Know It's Christmas? On 25 November dozens of British pop stars recorded it in a single day, including Bono, Sting, George Michael and Boy George. It became the fastest-selling single up to then in British history. The proceeds went to Ethiopia.
genres.listen: Each star sings a few lines. Try to recognise the voices: where do you hear Bono, and where Boy George?

genres.name: We Are the World
genres.text: On 28 January 1985, after the American Music Awards ceremony, 45 American stars came together in a studio in Los Angeles. Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie had written We Are the World, and Quincy Jones produced. On the door hung a note: check your ego at the door. The recording went on all night. The single sold millions of copies for the hungry in Africa.
genres.listen: Listen to how the voices take turns: Stevie Wonder, Bruce Springsteen, Cyndi Lauper, Bob Dylan. Each voice has a sound all its own.

genres.name: Gorbachev takes power
genres.text: On 11 March 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev became the leader of the Soviet Union. He was 54, much younger than his predecessors. With glasnost, openness, and perestroika, reform, he allowed more freedom. Western rock, which young people had first listened to secretly on copied cassettes, was increasingly permitted. Together with Reagan he talked about fewer nuclear weapons. In 1987 they signed a treaty.
genres.listen: In Russians Sting asks whether the Russians love their children too. He borrowed the melody from the Russian composer Prokofiev.

genres.name: Stock Aitken Waterman
genres.text: In March 1985 You Spin Me Round by Dead or Alive was at number one in England. It was the first big hit of Stock Aitken Waterman, three producers from London. They worked like a factory: a fast, tight rhythm, simple chords and a chorus that stuck at once. In their studio in south London they went on to make hits for Rick Astley, Bananarama, Kylie Minogue and Jason Donovan.
genres.listen: Hear the stomping bass, like a machine. With Venus by Bananarama, from 1986, they did the same with an old song by the Dutch band Shocking Blue.

genres.name: Modern Talking
genres.text: In the spring of 1985 You're My Heart, You're My Soul by the German duo Modern Talking spent six weeks at number one in West Germany. Dieter Bohlen wrote the song, Thomas Anders sang. It also became a hit in Austria, Switzerland, Belgium and the Netherlands, among others. It is an example of Eurodisco: danceable European pop music with synthesizers and a simple chorus. More than eight million copies have been sold worldwide.
genres.listen: Hear the high voices in the chorus, which answer Anders's singing, and the bouncing synthesizer bass beneath.

tracks.title: You're My Heart, You're My Soul

genres.name: Wham! in China
genres.text: On 7 April 1985 Wham!, the duo of George Michael and Andrew Ridgeley, gave a concert in Beijing, as the first Western pop group in communist China. The audience had never seen anything like it and did not quite know how to react. Manager Simon Napier-Bell had negotiated for months, also to get ahead of rival Queen. It was publicity for Wham!, but also an opening to a closed country.
genres.listen: This cheerful song is reminiscent of the soul of the sixties. The title comes from a note by Ridgeley, in which he accidentally wrote 'up up' and then, as a joke, added 'go go' after it.

tracks.title: Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go

genres.name: Dire Straits: Brothers in Arms
genres.text: In May 1985 Brothers in Arms by Dire Straits was released. The band recorded it largely in a studio on the Caribbean island of Montserrat, entirely digitally. It became the first album of which more than a million CDs were sold. Many people even bought a CD player for it. In the video for Money for Nothing Sting sings I want my MTV, and the little figures were made with a computer.
genres.listen: The song begins with a long, soft intro in which Sting sings I want my MTV. Then comes Mark Knopfler's raw guitar riff.

genres.name: The Atari ST
genres.text: In 1985 the Atari ST came on the market, a home computer with the MIDI connections already built in. With programs such as Notator and later Cubase you could put together a whole song on a screen: the computer then played back your synthesizers and drum machines. What had first needed an expensive studio could now be done in a bedroom. Many house and techno producers started that way.

genres.name: Live Aid
genres.text: On 13 July 1985 Live Aid was held, simultaneously at Wembley Stadium in London and JFK Stadium in Philadelphia. An estimated one and a half to two billion people watched worldwide. Phil Collins flew by Concorde to perform in both cities. The most talked-about performance was Queen's: over twenty minutes in which Freddie Mercury had 72,000 people singing along. Tens of millions of pounds were raised.
genres.listen: During Radio Ga Ga the whole of Wembley clapped above their heads at once, as in the video. The song is, of all things, about how television is displacing the radio.

genres.name: Jackson buys the Beatles
genres.text: In August 1985 Michael Jackson bought ATV Music for 47.5 million dollars, the company that held the rights to about 250 songs by Lennon and McCartney. Paul McCartney had also wanted to buy, but found it too expensive. Jackson had got the idea from McCartney in the first place, when McCartney told him how much money you earn from rights. Their friendship was over. Music became a possession to buy and sell.
genres.listen: In 1983 Jackson and McCartney had still released Say Say Say together, a cheerful duet. Two years later Jackson bought McCartney's songs.

genres.name: Pop lyrics before the Senate
genres.text: On 19 September 1985 Frank Zappa, Dee Snider of Twisted Sister and John Denver testified before the American Senate. A group of politicians' wives, the PMRC, found pop lyrics too violent and too sexual and had drawn up a list of fifteen offending songs, with Prince and Madonna on it too. The musicians defended freedom of speech. Even so a warning came on records, which later became the well-known Parental Advisory sticker.
genres.listen: We're Not Gonna Take It was on the list of fifteen. In the Senate Dee Snider said that the lyrics were simply about rebelliousness.

genres.name: Farm Aid
genres.text: At Live Aid Bob Dylan said that a small part of the money could also go to American farmers, who were losing their farms through debt. Willie Nelson, Neil Young and John Mellencamp took up that idea. On 22 September 1985 they held Farm Aid in Champaign, Illinois, for some 80,000 visitors. More than nine million dollars was raised for farming families. Farm Aid still exists.
genres.listen: Rain on the Scarecrow by Mellencamp tells of a farmer who loses his land to the bank. Hear the heavy, booming drums.

genres.name: Sun City
genres.text: On 16 October 1985 Sun City by Artists United Against Apartheid was released. Guitarist Steven Van Zandt brought together, among others, Bruce Springsteen, Bob Dylan, Miles Davis, Bono and Run-DMC. Sun City was a luxury holiday resort in South Africa, the country of apartheid, the legal separation of the races. Western stars performed there, despite a call for a boycott. In the song they promise never to play there. Many American radio stations did not play it.
genres.listen: Hear how rap, rock and funk run together. Each artist sings or raps a piece, and together they shout the chorus.

genres.name: a-ha: Take On Me
genres.text: Take On Me by the Norwegian a-ha flopped in England twice: first in 1984, and in April 1985 in a new recording by producer Alan Tarney. Warner in America gave director Steve Barron money for a remarkable video: a girl is drawn into a comic strip, drawn in pencil over filmed footage. That drawing work took months. MTV played the video again and again, and on 19 October 1985 a-ha was at number one in America.
genres.listen: Hear the riff on the synthesizer, which Magne Furuholmen had already come up with as a teenager. And then Morten Harket's high note in the chorus.

genres.name: Red Wedge
genres.text: On 21 November 1985 Red Wedge was founded in the British Houses of Parliament, a group of musicians around Billy Bragg and Paul Weller. They wanted to persuade young people to vote, and to vote Labour, against the government of Margaret Thatcher. At the start of 1986 they went on tour with The Style Council, The Communards and guests such as The Smiths and Madness. Even so Thatcher won the 1987 election.
genres.listen: Walls Come Tumbling Down! by The Style Council calls on people to rise up together. Hear Mick Talbot's rousing Hammond organ.

genres.name: Pet Shop Boys: West End Girls
genres.text: In January 1986 West End Girls by the Pet Shop Boys was at number one in England, and a few months later in America too. Neil Tennant was a journalist at the music magazine Smash Hits, Chris Lowe studied architecture. Tennant almost speaks the lyrics, like a rap. The song is about rich and poor in London. That is how synthpop became clever, dry and very British.
genres.listen: Hear how calm Tennant stays while the synthesizers and the rhythm grow fuller and fuller. The lyrics are partly inspired by a poem by T.S. Eliot.

genres.name: Europe: The Final Countdown
genres.text: On 14 February 1986 The Final Countdown by the Swedish rock band Europe was released. Singer Joey Tempest had come up with the synthesizer theme years earlier on a borrowed keyboard. The lyrics, about a departure into space, are inspired by Space Oddity by David Bowie. The song reached number one in 25 countries, including England and the Netherlands. Hard rock and synthesizer came together completely here.
genres.listen: The song begins with the synthesizer theme, played like a fanfare. Only then do the guitars and the drums join in.

genres.name: Metallica: Master of Puppets
genres.text: On 3 March 1986 Master of Puppets by Metallica was released. Thrash metal was faster, harder and more complicated than the hard rock on MTV, and hardly got on the radio. Even so the album, without a hit and without a video, sold hundreds of thousands of copies. Metallica had built up its fans with tours and with cassettes that fans copied among themselves. In September bassist Cliff Burton was killed in a bus accident in Sweden.
genres.listen: The song lasts over eight minutes and has a quiet middle section. It is about addiction: the drugs as a puppeteer pulling the strings.

genres.name: Falco: Rock Me Amadeus
genres.text: On 29 March 1986 Rock Me Amadeus by Falco from Vienna was at number one in America, as the first German-language song ever. The song tells the life of Mozart as that of a rock star: full of debts, in love and always at parties. Falco raps half in German, half in English. Mozart had just become famous again through the 1984 film Amadeus.
genres.listen: Hear how Falco speaks the lyrics more than he sings them, with a Viennese accent. The chorus, Amadeus Amadeus, is almost a chant.

genres.name: Peter Gabriel: Sledgehammer
genres.text: In 1986 Peter Gabriel made the video for Sledgehammer with the animation studio Aardman from Bristol, later known for Wallace & Gromit. Frame by frame Gabriel was filmed among dancing chickens, toy trains and fruit on his face. For this he had to lie still under a sheet of glass for hours. It became the video that MTV has broadcast most often, and it won nine MTV awards.
genres.listen: The song begins with the sound of a shakuhachi, a Japanese flute, from a sampler. Then brass and bass turn it into a soul song, in the style of the old soul records from Stax in Memphis.

genres.name: Chernobyl
genres.text: On 26 April 1986 a reactor of the nuclear power plant at Chernobyl in Ukraine, then part of the Soviet Union, exploded. A cloud of radioactive dust drifted over Europe, including the Netherlands. Farmers had to keep their cows indoors and vegetables from the garden were advised against. The Soviet government at first kept the accident secret. The disaster showed how dangerous nuclear energy could be, and how closed the country still was.

genres.name: Run-DMC and Aerosmith
genres.text: In July 1986 Run-DMC from Queens and the rock band Aerosmith released Walk This Way together, a rock song from 1975. In the video singer Steven Tyler literally breaks through the wall between two rehearsal rooms. The single reached number 4 in America and MTV played the video a lot. White rock fans discovered hip-hop, and Aerosmith, who had faded into obscurity, made a comeback.
genres.listen: The rappers rap the lyrics of Aerosmith, while Joe Perry plays his own guitar riff. Run-DMC had been rapping over the beginning of the record live for years, without really knowing the rest of the song.

genres.name: Bon Jovi: Slippery When Wet
genres.text: On 18 August 1986 Slippery When Wet by Bon Jovi from New Jersey was released. The band played hair metal: hard rock with big hair, catchy choruses and a lot of attention to the videos on MTV. Songwriter Desmond Child helped with the biggest hits. You Give Love a Bad Name and Livin' on a Prayer both reached number one in America, and the album spent eight weeks at the top.
genres.listen: Livin' on a Prayer is about Tommy and Gina, a young couple who struggle to make ends meet. Hear the talking effect on the guitar: a talk box, in which the guitar sound is shaped through a tube in the mouth.

tracks.title: You Give Love a Bad Name

genres.name: House at number one
genres.text: In January 1987 Jack Your Body by Steve 'Silk' Hurley from Chicago was at number one in England. It was the first house record to get that high. There is hardly any singing: just jack your body, a drum machine and a bassline. British young people who had never been to Chicago began playing and buying house. In a few months the music from the clubs of Chicago became a European craze.
genres.listen: Hear how the voice is cut into pieces and repeated with a sampler. That is how the word jack becomes an instrument.

genres.name: U2: The Joshua Tree
genres.text: On 9 March 1987 The Joshua Tree by U2 from Dublin was released. The band had already made a name with Sunday Bloody Sunday, about violence in Northern Ireland, and with Live Aid, where Bono climbed off the stage to dance with fans. The Joshua Tree was about America, faith and longing, and became their first number one in the United States. At the end of April U2 was on the cover of Time.
genres.listen: With or Without You builds up very slowly. The Edge's guitar lets notes ring on endlessly, with a device called the Infinite Guitar.

genres.name: Bowie at the Wall
genres.text: On 6 June 1987 David Bowie gave a concert in front of the Reichstag in West Berlin, close to the Wall. On the other side thousands of East German young people stood listening along. At Heroes, which Bowie had recorded in Berlin in 1977 about two lovers by the Wall, they sang along. The East German police stepped in. Six days later President Reagan called out at the Brandenburg Gate: Tear down this wall.
genres.listen: Heroes begins quietly and grows louder and louder; Bowie sings the last verses almost shouting. The screaming guitar is by Robert Fripp.

genres.name: Acid Tracks
genres.text: In 1987 Acid Tracks by Phuture was released, three boys from Chicago: DJ Pierre, Spanky and Herb J. Spanky had bought a second-hand Roland TB-303, a bass machine that nobody wanted. Turning the knobs while the pattern was running produced a squealing, squeaking sound. DJ Ron Hardy played the demo in his club Music Box. The crowd called it acid, and so it was called from then on.
genres.listen: For over twelve minutes you hear almost only a drum machine and the 303. Notice how the sound slowly changes, becoming sharper and dirtier.

genres.name: Guns N' Roses
genres.text: On 21 July 1987 Appetite for Destruction by Guns N' Roses from Los Angeles was released. The album at first sold badly, until MTV began broadcasting the video for Welcome to the Jungle and viewers asked for more. It became the best-selling debut album in America. After years of hairspray and glossy rock videos, this band sounded dangerous again.
genres.listen: Slash's guitar figure in Sweet Child o' Mine began as a joke, a finger exercise in the rehearsal room. Axl Rose wrote a love song to go with it.

genres.name: MTV Europe
genres.text: On 1 August 1987, exactly six years after the American channel, MTV Europe began with a party in Amsterdam. The first video was Money for Nothing by Dire Straits, with the words I want my MTV. Via cable and satellite the channel reached more and more European living rooms. The presenters spoke English and came from different countries. Young people all over Europe now watched the same videos.

genres.name: Pump Up the Volume
genres.text: In October 1987 Pump Up the Volume by M|A|R|R|S was at number one in England. The song was a patchwork of samples: pieces from dozens of other records, from James Brown to an Israeli singer. It was one of the first big hits made that way. Stock Aitken Waterman, a piece of whose work was also used, went to court. Sampling became a matter for lawyers.
genres.listen: Try to recognise the samples: a voice saying pump up the volume, Israeli singing, scratch sounds. Everything belongs to someone else, the combination is new.

genres.name: Kylie Minogue
genres.text: Kylie Minogue was known in Australia as an actress in the soap Neighbours. When she came to London in 1987, Stock Aitken Waterman had forgotten they had an appointment. According to the story they wrote I Should Be So Lucky in forty minutes while she sat waiting. In February 1988 it was at number one. In those years SAW sometimes had several songs in the Top 10 at once.
genres.listen: The song is about someone who is only lucky in love in her dreams. Hear how the chorus stays in your head at once.

genres.name: Mandela concert at Wembley
genres.text: On 11 June 1988 a concert was given at Wembley for the seventieth birthday of Nelson Mandela, who was still in prison. It was broadcast in dozens of countries. When Stevie Wonder could not perform because a computer disk with his music was missing, the still unknown Tracy Chapman was allowed on stage a second time, alone with her guitar. After that Fast Car became a hit.
genres.listen: Fast Car is about a girl who wants to escape poverty with her boyfriend. Hear the guitar figure that keeps returning, like a car that keeps driving.

genres.name: Acid house in England
genres.text: In September 1987 four London DJs, including Paul Oakenfold and Danny Rampling, went on holiday to Ibiza. In the open-air club Amnesia they heard DJ Alfredo mix house, pop and Italian records. Back in London Rampling started the club Shoom. In 1988 the Second Summer of Love followed: raves in warehouses and meadows, smileys on T-shirts and young people dancing until morning.
genres.listen: We Call It Acieed by D-Mob became a hit in October 1988, just as newspapers linked acid house to drugs. Hear how singer Gary Haisman keeps shouting Acieed, like a cry on the dance floor.

genres.name: Public Enemy
genres.text: On 28 June 1988 It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back by Public Enemy was released. The production team The Bomb Squad stacked dozens of samples on top of each other: sirens, squealing saxophones, speeches and pieces of James Brown. Chuck D called rap the CNN of black America, the news you heard nowhere else. In 1989 came Fight the Power, for the film Do the Right Thing by Spike Lee.
genres.listen: In Fight the Power, hear how many sounds play at the same time. The lyrics attack Elvis and John Wayne as heroes of white America.

genres.name: Springsteen in East Berlin
genres.text: On 19 July 1988 Bruce Springsteen played in East Berlin, at a cycling track in Weißensee. The communist government hoped to keep the young people content, but hundreds of thousands of people turned up. Springsteen gave a short speech in halting German: he hoped that one day all barriers would be torn down. Then he played Chimes of Freedom by Bob Dylan. A little over a year later the Wall fell.
genres.listen: Springsteen released his live version of Chimes of Freedom in 1988. Dylan's lyrics are about freedom for everyone who is left out.

genres.name: Yo! MTV Raps
genres.text: On 6 August 1988 MTV in America began Yo! MTV Raps, a programme with only hip-hop videos. The makers expected little, but it became one of the channel's most-watched programmes. The presenter was Fab 5 Freddy, a graffiti artist from Brooklyn. So young people far from New York, in Europe too, saw every week what rappers looked like, how they talked and how they dressed.

genres.name: Techno from Detroit
genres.text: In the summer of 1988 Inner City from Detroit had a worldwide hit with Big Fun. Producer Kevin Saunderson was one of the Belleville Three, three friends from a suburb of Detroit who took inspiration from Kraftwerk and the empty factories of their city. Their music was called techno: barer and cooler than house. With singer Paris Grey, Saunderson made cheerful pop music of it instead.
genres.listen: Compare the tight drum machine with Paris Grey's warm voice: machine and human together. Good Life followed a few months later.

genres.name: Madonna, Pepsi and Like a Prayer
genres.text: On 2 March 1989 Pepsi broadcast a commercial in which Madonna sang Like a Prayer. A day later the real video appeared on MTV, with burning crosses and a statue of a saint that comes to life. Churches were furious and called for a boycott. Pepsi dropped the commercial, but Madonna was allowed to keep the money. She had shown that uproar was good for sales.
genres.listen: The song has a gospel choir and begins with a guitar that is abruptly cut off. Hear how pop and faith run together here.

genres.name: The Game Boy
genres.text: On 21 April 1989 the Game Boy came out in Japan, a portable games console from Nintendo. In America and Europe it was supplied with Tetris, with the Russian folk song Korobeiniki as its music. So in millions of pockets there was a Russian melody, played by a squeaking sound chip. Later musicians used the Game Boy itself as an instrument, for chiptune.

genres.name: Rock in Moscow
genres.text: On 12 and 13 August 1989 Bon Jovi, Mötley Crüe, Ozzy Osbourne and the Scorpions played in the Lenin Stadium in Moscow, at the Moscow Music Peace Festival. Under Gorbachev the Soviet Union opened up more and more. Klaus Meine of the Scorpions saw soldiers and fans partying together and shortly afterwards wrote Wind of Change. It became the song of the end of the Cold War.
genres.listen: The song begins with whistling, by Meine himself. He sings about a walk along the Moskva river, while the wind of change blows.

genres.name: The Wall falls
genres.text: On the evening of 9 November 1989 the border crossings in the Berlin Wall unexpectedly opened. Thousands of East Berliners walked to the west, people climbed on the Wall and chipped pieces out of it. On New Year's Eve David Hasselhoff, star of the TV series Knight Rider, sang Looking for Freedom at the Brandenburg Gate, in a jacket with lights. The Cold War was coming to an end.
genres.listen: Looking for Freedom was number one in West Germany for weeks in 1989. It is a German schlager song from 1978, which Hasselhoff recorded again.

genres.name: Mandela free
genres.text: On 11 February 1990 Nelson Mandela walked out of prison a free man after 27 years. Two months later, on 16 April, he himself stood on the stage at Wembley at a concert in honour of his release. Musicians had made his name known for years. In 1994 he became the first black president of South Africa.
genres.listen: Hugh Masekela from South Africa wrote Bring Him Back Home in 1987, with a trumpet melody that sounds like a parade.

genres.name: Milli Vanilli exposed
genres.text: In mid-November 1990 producer Frank Farian announced that Rob Pilatus and Fab Morvan of Milli Vanilli had never sung on their records themselves. They had even won a Grammy with them that year, for best new artist. It was taken away from them again. In the 1980s a pop star was sometimes mainly a face for the video, and the voice came from someone else.
genres.listen: Listen closely: the voices belong to studio singers. In the video only the lips of Rob and Fab move.

genres.name: Nirvana: Nevermind
genres.text: On 24 September 1991 Nevermind by Nirvana from Seattle was released. Smells Like Teen Spirit sounded raw and angry, with guitars that went from soft to very loud. The video, in a school gym with anarchist cheerleaders, made the glossy rock videos of the 1980s old-fashioned in one stroke. In January 1992 Nevermind pushed the album Dangerous by Michael Jackson off the top spot.
genres.listen: Listen to the difference between the quiet verse and the loud chorus. Kurt Cobain said he was trying to imitate the band Pixies.
